lead: A closed section beam is a box: its wall forms one continuous loop, so shear flow has no free edge to start from. The trick is to cut the loop once in imagination, treat the result as an open section and compute the basic shear flow q<sub>b</sub>. The real section is q<sub>b</sub> plus a constant q<sub>0</sub> round the loop. q<sub>0</sub> is fixed by the twist condition: a shear force through the shear centre causes no twist. Aircraft fuselages, wing boxes and car bodies use this calculation to place the shear centre and avoid unwanted torsion.
prereq: You need Chapter 5.2 for qb of an open section and Chapter 5.4 for the zero-twist condition in Bredt form.

sections.h3: The cut and the constant q₀

blocks.text: In a closed thin-walled beam the wall forms one loop, so q cannot start from a free edge. Make an imaginary cut through one wall. The cut is a calculation device, not a physical slit. It turns the box into an open section, and 5.2 gives the basic shear flow q<sub>b</sub> in N/mm. Set q<sub>b</sub> = 0 at the cut and integrate round the mean line. Typical aircraft boxes use skins 1–3 mm thick and cell sizes 100–400 mm.

The real closed section carries q = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>0</sub>. q<sub>0</sub> is a constant shear flow all round the loop, in N/mm. It replaces the connection removed by the cut. It is not found from statics of the cut section; it comes from compatibility.

blocks.where: q<sub>b</sub> is basic shear flow (N/mm); t is wall thickness (mm); ds is element of mean-line length (mm); ∮ is one complete loop. For uniform t, q₀ = −(1/L)∮q<sub>b</sub> ds, where L is perimeter (mm).

blocks.text: For a shear load through the shear centre, the correct twist is zero: ∮(q/t)ds = 0. Substitute q = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>0</sub> and solve. If t varies, keep t in both integrals. After q<sub>0</sub> is added, check that the resultant of q equals the applied shear and acts through the shear centre. Torque-carrying closed sections are in 5.4.

items: Choose any point on the mean line as the cut. Mark a positive direction round the loop.
Compute I<sub>x</sub> about the centroidal axis normal to the shear force, using mean-line dimensions.
Start at the cut with q<sub>b</sub> = 0. Integrate q<sub>b</sub> = −(S/I<sub>x</sub>)∫ t y ds along the path; y is distance from the centroidal axis.
Integrate q<sub>b</sub> once round the loop. For uniform t, q<sub>0</sub> = −(∮q<sub>b</sub> ds)/L.
Add q<sub>0</sub> to every q<sub>b</sub>. Check ∮(q/t)ds = 0.
Take moments of q about a point O. The shear centre offset is e = M<sub>O</sub>/S.

blocks.text: The cut can be at a corner, mid-wall or on a flange. q<sub>b</sub> changes with the cut, but q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>0</sub> does not. At the cut the real shear flow is q<sub>0</sub>, not zero. For one axis of symmetry the shear centre lies on that axis; for two axes it is at the centroid. An unsymmetrical section needs S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub> components and moments about two axes.

Symmetrical boxes are the common wing-box and fuselage case. A vertical shear through the vertical symmetry axis gives q values equal and opposite on the two sides. q<sub>0</sub> shifts the loop so twist is zero; the shear centre lies on the symmetry axis. One moment equation locates it along that axis.

An unsymmetrical closed section needs both shear components. Compute q<sub>b</sub> for S<sub>x</sub> and S<sub>y</sub>, add one q<sub>0</sub> from the combined zero-twist condition, then take moments about two reference axes. The resultant of q is the shear force through the shear centre. If the real load is elsewhere, the offset times load is a torque; that torsion problem is in 5.4 and 5.5. The same moment check also confirms that the applied shear equals the resultant of q.

figure.caption: The cut is imaginary: q<sub>b</sub> is zero only in the cut-open section; adding a constant q<sub>0</sub> makes the closed section twist-free under a shear force through the shear centre.

examples.question: A rectangular closed box has mean-line width b = 200 mm, depth h = 100 mm and uniform skin thickness t = 2 mm. It carries a vertical shear force S = 10 kN through the mid-point of the left vertical wall. Taking a clockwise positive path from an imaginary cut at the mid-height of the left wall, find: (a) q<sub>b</sub> at the four corners; (b) q<sub>0</sub>; (c) the distance of the shear centre from the left wall. Use thin-walled theory.
steps: Cut at mid-left. q<sub>b</sub> = 0 at the cut. On the upper left wall, ∫t y ds = 2∫₀⁵⁰ y dy = 2500 mm³. q<sub>b</sub>(top-left) = −k×2500 = −10.71 N/mm. By symmetry q<sub>b</sub>(bottom-left) = −10.71 N/mm.
Top flange adds ∫t y ds = 2×50×200 = 20,000 mm³. q<sub>b</sub>(top-right) = −k(2500 + 20,000) = −96.43 N/mm. By symmetry q<sub>b</sub>(bottom-right) = −96.43 N/mm.
Evaluate once round the loop: ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds = −3.214×10⁴ N. Perimeter L = 2(200 + 100) = 600 mm. q<sub>0</sub> = −(−3.214×10⁴)/600 = +53.57 N/mm.
Final q = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>0</sub>. Left corners: −10.71 + 53.57 = +42.86 N/mm. Right corners: −96.43 + 53.57 = −42.86 N/mm. Check: ∮(q/t)ds = 0.

Take moments about mid-left wall O. Left wall has zero arm; top and bottom flange moments cancel. On the right wall, ∫q ds = q<sub>0</sub>×100 + ∫q<sub>b</sub> ds = 5357.1 − 10,357.1 = −5000 N. Moment magnitude = 200×5000 = 1.000×10⁶ N·mm. e = M<sub>O</sub>/S = 1.000×10⁶/10,000 = 100 mm.
examples.answer: q<sub>b</sub> = −10.71 N/mm at top-left and bottom-left, −96.43 N/mm at top-right and bottom-right; q<sub>0</sub> = +53.57 N/mm; the shear centre lies 100 mm to the right of the left wall, at mid-depth.
examples.check:
b = 200.0
h = 100.0
t = 2.0
S = 10000.0
I = t*h**3/6 + b*t*h**2/2
k = S/I
qb_tl = -k*t*(h/2)**2/2
qb_tr = qb_tl - k*t*(h/2)*b
n = 20000
q = 0.0
total = 0.0
for i in range(n):
    y0 = (h/2)*i/n
    y1 = (h/2)*(i+1)/n
    ds = y1-y0
    ym = (y0+y1)/2
    q += -k*t*ym*ds
    total += q*ds
for i in range(n):
    ds = b/n
    q += -k*t*(h/2)*ds
    total += q*ds
for i in range(n):
    ds = h/n
    ym = h/2 - h*(i+0.5)/n
    q += -k*t*ym*ds
    total += q*ds
for i in range(n):
    ds = b/n
    q += -k*t*(-h/2)*ds
    total += q*ds
for i in range(n):
    y0 = -h/2 + (h/2)*i/n
    y1 = -h/2 + (h/2)*(i+1)/n
    ds = y1-y0
    ym = (y0+y1)/2
    q += -k*t*ym*ds
    total += q*ds
L = 2*(b+h)
q0 = -total/L
q_left = qb_tl + q0
q_right = qb_tr + q0
e = b/2
print(f"{qb_tl:.3f}")
print(f"{qb_tr:.3f}")
print(f"{q0:.3f}")
print(f"{q_left:.3f}")
print(f"{q_right:.3f}")
print(f"{e:.3f}")

traps: Forgetting q<sub>0</sub> and using the open-section q<sub>b</sub> as the real closed-section shear flow.
Assuming q = 0 at a chosen corner or cut in the real closed section; q<sub>0</sub> shifts every value.
Mixing sign conventions: q<sub>b</sub> and q<sub>0</sub> must use the same positive direction round the loop.
Using ∮q ds = 0 instead of ∮(q/t)ds = 0 when the wall thickness is not uniform.
Finding the shear centre from the centroid alone in an unsymmetrical closed section instead of taking moments of the q distribution.

quiz.q: What is q<sub>0</sub> in the shear flow of a closed section?
quiz.a: A constant shear flow, in N/mm, added all round the cut-open loop so that the real closed section satisfies the twist condition.

quiz.q: Why is the cut in a closed-section shear calculation called imaginary?
quiz.a: The real section has no free edge. The cut is made only to calculate q<sub>b</sub>; q<sub>0</sub> restores the loop, so the cut point is not physically open.

quiz.q: If q<sub>b</sub> at the cut is set to zero and q<sub>0</sub> = 40 N/mm, what is the real shear flow at the cut?
quiz.a: q = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>0</sub> = 0 + 40 = 40 N/mm. The real section does not have zero shear flow there.

quiz.q: A uniform-skin closed loop has ∮q<sub>b</sub> ds = −30,000 N and perimeter L = 600 mm. Find q<sub>0</sub>.
quiz.a: For uniform t, q<sub>0</sub> = −(∮q<sub>b</sub> ds)/L = −(−30,000)/600 = +50 N/mm.

quiz.q: Why does a shear load through the shear centre require ∮(q/t)ds = 0?
quiz.a: A load through the shear centre produces no twist. The twist of a closed section under shear flow q is proportional to ∮(q/t)ds, so setting this integral to zero removes twist and fixes q<sub>0</sub>.

quiz.q: A student cuts a rectangular box at a corner and sets q = 0 there in the final distribution. What is wrong?
quiz.a: q = 0 only in the cut-open calculation. The real closed section has q = q<sub>b</sub> + q<sub>0</sub>; at the corner q<sub>b</sub> may be zero but q<sub>0</sub> is generally not zero.

quiz.q: For a doubly symmetric rectangular closed box, where is the shear centre?
quiz.a: At the centroid, on both axes of symmetry, when the walls are uniform and thin-walled.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, closed-section shear flow feeds directly into finite-element shell models of wing boxes and fuselage barrels. Optimisation tools vary skin thickness round the loop to move the shear centre and reduce trim drag. Multi-cell wing boxes add one equal-twist equation per cell, which is the natural next step after this chapter. Search next for shear centre of unsymmetrical closed sections, Bredt-Batho shear flow and multi-cell shear flow.
